blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Explain what the Consumer Prices Index is, calculate a yearly inflation rate from it, and read what a change in the index means for a fixed sum of money.

blocks.heading: The basket and its weights
blocks.text: The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) measures the general price level by tracking the cost of a fixed basket of goods and services a typical household buys - mahangu meal, bus fares, rent, clothing - with each item weighted by the share of household spending it takes. The index number has no unit of its own: an index of 120.0 means the basket costs 120% of what it cost in the base year. Statistics offices reweight the basket from household spending surveys as habits shift, as the Dutch statistics office does each year for the Netherlands.

blocks.heading: Two rates worked out
blocks.text: The yearly inflation rate is the percentage rise in the CPI over a year. Worked: the CPI moves from 120.0 to 126.0. Step one: 126.0 - 120.0 = 6.0 index points. Step two: 6.0 / 120.0 = 0.05. Step three: 0.05 x 100 = 5, so prices rose 5% that year. A falling index works the same way. The CPI moves from 120.0 to 117.6. The change is 117.6 - 120.0 = -2.4 index points. Then -2.4 / 120.0 = -0.02. So -0.02 x 100 = -2: the general price level fell 2% that year, which is deflation.

blocks.heading: One index, different households
blocks.text: The CPI is one average, and the average conceals a spread. Where food prices rise 12% while clothing rises 2%, a household spending a large share of its income on food faces a faster rise in its cost of living than the index shows, and a household spending little on food faces a slower one. The measured rate depends on the basket: an Oshakati household and a Windhoek professional household share the same index but live different price rises.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The index turns the general price level into a number the price stability aim of topic 4.1 can be judged against, and the interest rates of topic 4.4 are set with it in view.
